items.prompt: Every sound is made by something ___.
hints: Touch your throat gently while you hum.
Pluck a stretched rubber band and watch it closely.
The word means moving quickly backwards and forwards. It starts with the letter v.
items.explanation: Every sound is made by something vibrating, which means moving quickly backwards and forwards. The vibrations travel through the air to our ears.

items.prompt: Match each instrument to the part that vibrates to make its sound.
hints: Ask which part of each instrument you pluck, hit, blow into or shake.
In a wind instrument, it is the air that vibrates.
Start with the guitar. Think about what you pluck with your fingers.
items.explanation: Guitar strings, drum skins and metal gongs vibrate when they are plucked or struck. In a flute the air inside the tube vibrates, and an angklung's bamboo tubes vibrate when it is shaken.

items.prompt: Ari puts his ear on one end of a table. Beni gently taps the other end. Ari hears the tap clearly. What does this show?

options.text: Sound can only travel through air.
options.why: Ari's ear was pressed on the table, so the sound came through the wood.

options.text: Tables make their own sounds.
options.why: The table only carried the vibrations from Beni's tap.

options.text: Sound can travel through solids.
Sound can only travel through water.
options.why: Sound travels through solids, liquids and gases.

hints: Ari's ear is touching the table, not open to the air.
The tap makes the wood vibrate.
Ask what the vibrations travelled through to reach Ari's ear.
items.explanation: The tap makes the table vibrate, and the vibrations travel through the solid wood to Ari's ear. Sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases.

items.prompt: How can you make a drum sound louder?

options.text: Hit it more gently.
options.why: Gentle taps make small vibrations and quieter sounds.

options.text: Tighten the skin.
options.why: Tightening the skin makes the pitch higher. It does not make the drum louder.

options.text: Put a cloth on the skin.
options.why: A cloth muffles the drum and makes it quieter.

options.text: Hit it harder, so the skin makes bigger vibrations.

hints: Loudness depends on the size of the vibrations.
Bigger vibrations carry more energy to your ears.
Think about what you do with the stick to make a big vibration.
items.explanation: Hitting the drum harder makes the skin vibrate with bigger movements, so the sound is louder. Changing how tight the skin is changes the pitch instead.

items.prompt: Sort these into higher pitch and lower pitch.
hints: Pitch means how high or low a note sounds.
Faster vibrations make higher notes. Short, thin or tight things vibrate faster.
Compare the two angklung tubes first.
items.explanation: Short, thin, tight or small things vibrate faster and make higher notes. Long, thick, loose or large things vibrate more slowly and make lower notes.

items.prompt: Nina has four identical bottles with different amounts of water. She blows across the top of each one. Which bottle makes the highest note?

options.text: the bottle with the least water
options.why: That bottle has the longest column of air, which vibrates slowly and gives a low note.

options.text: the bottle with the most water
the bottle that is half full
options.why: It has more air inside than the fullest bottle, so its note is lower.

options.text: all four bottles make the same note
options.why: The column of air is a different length in each bottle, so the notes are different.

hints: When you blow across a bottle, the air inside it vibrates.
A shorter column of air vibrates faster and makes a higher note.
Find the bottle with the smallest space of air above the water.
items.explanation: Blowing makes the air in the bottle vibrate. The bottle with the most water has the shortest column of air, which vibrates fastest and gives the highest note.

items.prompt: Choose all the materials that would help to muffle sound in a music room.

options.text: thick curtains
carpet
foam panels
glass windows
options.why: Hard, smooth glass reflects sound instead of soaking it up.

options.text: metal sheets
options.why: Hard metal reflects sound, so the room would echo more.

hints: Muffling means soaking up sound so less of it bounces around.
Soft materials with lots of tiny air gaps absorb sound well.
For each material, ask whether it is soft and squashy or hard and smooth.
items.explanation: Soft materials such as curtains, carpet and foam absorb sound, so they muffle it. Hard, smooth surfaces such as glass and metal reflect sound back into the room.

items.prompt: Many small bats hunt insects in the dark. How do they find the insects?

options.text: They make high sounds and listen for the echoes that bounce back.
They see light given out by every insect.
options.why: Most insects do not glow, so the bats use sound to find them.

options.text: They smell each insect from far away.
options.why: These bats find flying insects using echoes of their own calls.

options.text: They feel the insects with their wings.
options.why: The insects are too far away to touch until the bat catches them.

hints: An echo is a sound that bounces back off a surface.
These bats make calls that are too high for people to hear.
Think about what happens when a bat's call hits an insect in front of it.
items.explanation: Insect-eating bats make very high sounds that bounce off insects as echoes. By listening to the echoes, the bats can tell where the insects are, even in the dark.

items.prompt: Astronauts on a spacewalk use radios to talk to each other. Why can they not hear each other shout?

options.text: Space is too cold for sound to work.
options.why: Temperature is not the problem. Sound needs a material to travel through.

options.text: Sound travels too fast in space to hear.
options.why: Sound cannot travel through empty space at all.

options.text: Space is almost empty, so nothing carries the sound vibrations.
Shouting makes no vibrations in a spacesuit.
options.why: Their voices still vibrate, but nothing outside the suits passes the vibrations on.

hints: Sound travels as vibrations passed from particle to particle.
Think about what fills the space between two astronauts outside a spacecraft.
Ask what sound needs to travel through, and whether space has it.
items.explanation: Sound needs a material, such as air, water or a solid, to pass its vibrations along. Space is almost empty, so sound cannot travel through it, but radio signals can.

items.prompt: Nina has four identical glass bottles with different amounts of water. She taps each one with a metal spoon. Which bottle makes the highest note?

options.text: the bottle with the most water
options.why: When you tap, the glass and the water vibrate together. More water makes slower vibrations and a lower note.

options.text: all four bottles make the same note
options.why: Each bottle holds a different amount of water, so each one vibrates differently.

options.text: the bottle that is half full
options.why: It has more water than the emptiest bottle, so its note is lower.

options.text: the bottle with the least water

hints: Tapping makes the glass vibrate, together with the water inside it.
More water makes the vibrating bottle heavier, so it vibrates more slowly.
Compare this with blowing across the bottles, where the column of air vibrates.
items.explanation: When you tap a bottle, the glass and the water inside it vibrate. Less water means faster vibrations, so the bottle with the least water gives the highest note, the opposite of blowing.
